client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just can't seem to enjoy it the way I used to — it's like her absence is this huge shadow hanging over everything. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how I feel, but I figured I'd give this a try.
therapist: I'm really glad you decided to give this a try, and I want you to know that what you're feeling makes complete sense — losing your grandmother and then facing family gatherings without her presence is a profound kind of grief. That "shadow" you described is such a meaningful way to put it, and it tells me how central she was to those moments of connection for you. I'm curious — when you're at one of those gatherings and that feeling washes over you, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind in those moments?

client: It's mostly things like "she should be here right now" or "nothing is ever going to feel the same again." And then I start feeling guilty, like I'm ruining the moment for everyone else by being sad, even though I'm trying to hold it together on the outside. It's this weird combination of grief and guilt that just makes me want to leave early and be alone.
therapist: Those thoughts — "she should be here" and "nothing will feel the same" — are such a natural part of grief, and it makes sense they'd pull you away from the present moment, but I also notice that the guilt on top of the grief sounds like it's creating a second layer of pain that's almost harder to carry. It's worth gently questioning that guilt — is there any real evidence that your sadness is actually ruining the experience for others, or might that be your mind adding an extra burden during an already tender time? I wonder, if a close family member told you they were quietly grieving at a gathering, would you feel they were ruining it for you?

client: No, I wouldn't feel that way at all — I'd actually want to comfort them. But it's harder to apply that same logic to myself, because it just feels different when it's me. Like I know intellectually what you're saying makes sense, but in the moment at those gatherings, the guilt still hits just as hard regardless of what I logically know.
therapist: What you're describing — that gap between knowing something logically and actually *feeling* it in the moment — is one of the most human and frustrating parts of grief, and it doesn't mean you're doing anything wrong. That compassion you'd so naturally offer a family member is actually still available to you; it just needs some practice to turn inward, especially when emotions are running high. I'm wondering, in those moments at gatherings when the guilt starts to rise, is there anything — even something small — that has ever helped you feel even a tiny bit more gentle toward yourself?

client: Honestly, I'm struggling to think of anything that really helps in those moments. Sometimes stepping outside for a few minutes gives me a tiny bit of relief, but then I come back in and feel guilty about that too, like I abandoned everyone. It's like there's no escape from the guilt no matter what I do.
therapist: It sounds like guilt has become almost like a trap where even the one thing that brings you a little relief — stepping outside — gets turned into another reason to feel bad, and that's exhausting. I want to gently offer a reframe: stepping outside for a few minutes isn't abandoning anyone, it's actually you taking care of yourself so you *can* be present, which takes real courage when you're grieving. What do you think your grandmother would say if she knew you were stepping outside for a moment to collect yourself in her memory?

client: She would probably tell me to stop being so hard on myself — she was always the one in the family who gave people permission to feel what they needed to feel. But even knowing that, it almost makes it worse in a way, because it reminds me that she's not there to actually say it to me anymore. I guess I never realized how much I relied on her for that kind of reassurance.
therapist: What a beautiful and profound thing to recognize — that she was your source of permission to feel, and now you're discovering that you need to find a way to carry that gift she gave you *within yourself*. It makes complete sense that realizing her role brings a fresh wave of loss, and that's not a setback — it's actually a deeper layer of grief that deserves its own space. I'm wondering, are there small ways you might begin to act as that voice for yourself — almost like honoring her by treating yourself the way she would have treated you?

client: I like the idea of it, but I honestly don't know how to do that in practice — it sounds nice in theory but in the moment I'm just flooded with emotion and I can't think clearly enough to be my own reassuring voice. It feels a little like being told to be your own best friend when you're drowning. I guess I'm worried that trying to channel her will just make me miss her more instead of actually helping.
therapist: That "drowning" image is really important — it tells me that in those flooded moments, we can't ask your mind to do complex emotional work, and trying to force it could feel like one more thing to fail at. So rather than channeling her in the thick of it, I wonder if we could think smaller — like a single word or a brief physical gesture that carries her presence, something you could access even when you're overwhelmed, almost like a tiny anchor she left behind. Is there a word she used, or something she did — a touch on the arm, a particular phrase — that instantly brings her warmth to mind?

client: She used to call me "sweetheart" in this very specific, unhurried way — not like how people throw the word around, but like she really meant it and had all the time in the world for you. Just thinking about it now actually does bring a little warmth, but I'm also scared that if I use it as some kind of technique, it'll start to feel mechanical and lose what makes it special. I don't want to turn something genuine into a coping strategy, if that makes sense.
therapist: That fear makes complete sense, and it actually speaks to how deeply you want to protect what was real between you — that's love, not resistance. But I'd gently offer that carrying her "sweetheart" with you into hard moments isn't diminishing it; it might actually be the most alive way to keep that genuine connection breathing in your everyday life. I'm curious — do you think she would have wanted that word to stay locked away safely, or to be there for you exactly when you needed it most?

client: When you put it that way, I think she would have wanted me to use it — she wasn't the type to hoard love, she gave it freely. But I still feel a little uncertain, like what if I try it at the next family gathering and it just makes me break down crying in front of everyone, which is exactly what I've been trying to avoid. I don't want to test it out for the first time in a room full of people.
therapist: That's such wise self-awareness — recognizing that a crowded family gathering isn't the right place for a first experiment with something this tender. What if you tried it somewhere safe and private first, maybe just sitting quietly at home, letting yourself hear that word and whatever feelings come with it, so it's not completely uncharted territory when you're around others? That way you're not avoiding it, but you're also not throwing yourself into the deep end — you're giving yourself the same unhurried care she always gave you.

client: That actually feels more manageable than what I was imagining — I think I was picturing having to use it perfectly in a high-pressure moment right away. But I'll be honest, I'm a little worried that sitting alone with it might just turn into a full crying session where I spiral, and then I'll feel worse instead of better. I guess I don't fully trust myself to handle what might come up when there's no one around to help me through it.
therapist: That fear of spiraling alone is really valid, and it's worth knowing that crying — even a lot of it — isn't the same as spiraling; sometimes it's actually grief doing exactly what it needs to do. But we can build in a small safety net: you might try it for just a few minutes with a clear, gentle endpoint planned, like making yourself a cup of tea afterward, so there's a soft landing waiting for you rather than an open-ended unknown. What would help you feel just enough supported to try it — is there someone you could text afterward, or a small ritual that would help you feel held even when you're on your own?

client: There's my cousin who was also really close to her — I think she'd understand if I reached out after. But I'm realizing as I say that, that I've been avoiding talking to her about all of this because I don't want to make her sad too, which I guess is that same guilt pattern showing up again. Maybe texting her afterward could actually be good for both of us, though I'm still not entirely sure I'm ready to open that door.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you just caught that guilt pattern in real time — that's actually a significant moment of self-awareness, and it suggests you're starting to recognize how that voice operates before it fully takes hold. There's something quietly beautiful in the possibility that reaching out to your cousin isn't burdening her, but offering her the same connection your grandmother modeled — that generous, unhurried love that didn't hoard itself. I'm wondering, what would "ready enough" look like for you — not perfectly ready, but just enough to take that small step toward her?
